title: Predicting onset of symptomatic Alzheimerʼs disease with plasma p-tau217 clocks

authors.name: Erin G. Rosenbaugh
authors.affiliation: Foundation for the National Institutes of Health

authors.name: J. Martin Sabandal
authors.affiliation: Foundation for the National Institutes of Health

abstract: Abstract Predicting not just if, but also when, cognitively unimpaired individuals are likely to develop onset of Alzheimerʼs disease (AD) symptoms would be useful to clinical trials and, eventually, clinical practice. Although clock models based on amyloid and tau positron emission tomography have shown promise in predicting the onset of AD symptoms, a model based on plasma biomarkers would be more accessible. Using longitudinal plasma %p-tau217 (the ratio of phosphorylated to non-phosphorylated tau at position 217) from two independent cohorts ( n = 258 and n = 345), clock models were used to estimate the age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity. The estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity was associated with the age at onset of AD symptoms (adjusted R 2 of 0.337−0.612) with a median absolute error of 3.0−3.7 years. Notably, the time from %p-tau217 positivity to onset of AD symptoms was markedly shorter in older individuals. Similar models were constructed with data from one p-tau217/Aβ42 immunoassay and four plasma p-tau217 immunoassays. These findings suggest that the time until onset of AD symptoms can be estimated using a single blood test within a margin of error that is acceptable for use in clinical trials.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This Nature Medicine article has already shown strong scholarly traction: it has 31 OpenAlex citations, sits in the top 1% of works in its field and year, and has been reused in 32 downstream works. The record also shows early public and teaching uptake, including one Bluesky mention and four YouTube videos that explicitly linked to the paper.

Full narrative

The paper’s central contribution is a practical one: it extends Alzheimer’s disease “clock” modeling to plasma p-tau217, aiming to predict not only whether cognitively unimpaired individuals may develop symptoms, but when. That framing aligns closely with the article’s citation pattern, which is concentrated in Alzheimer’s disease and dementia research but already reaches adjacent biomarker and assay-development communities. The work is being cited by articles, preprints, a review, and a conference paper, suggesting use across both discovery and translational contexts.

The citation record is especially notable for a 2026 Nature Medicine article: almost all recorded citations arrived in 2026, indicating rapid uptake soon after publication. The citing landscape includes work in medRxiv and Nature Medicine, as well as journals focused on neurology, diagnostics, and biomarker methods. In other words, the article is being read not only as an Alzheimer’s disease study, but also as part of a broader shift toward minimally invasive blood-based prediction tools.

Public and pedagogical signals are modest but present. There is one recorded Bluesky post discussing the study, and four YouTube videos explicitly linked the paper in their metadata or description, indicating that it has begun to circulate in educational and explanatory settings. Those signals do not replace scholarly citation, but they do show that the article is being used to communicate an evolving idea about Alzheimer’s prediction beyond the specialist literature.

At the same time, the post-publication record shows active scrutiny: PubPeer lists four threads for the article, which means the paper has also drawn methodological or interpretive attention. The scite record includes one supporting citation statement and many mentioning statements, so the literature is engaging with the work, but the citation discourse is still developing. Funding from NIH/NIA, the Alzheimer’s Association, and industry partners, together with linked GitHub repositories, suggests that the study sits within a well-resourced and methodologically transparent biomarker ecosystem.

Overall, the strongest story is one of early and unusually fast scholarly adoption for a biomarker paper with clear translational relevance. The paper is already influencing how researchers think about blood-based prediction of Alzheimer’s symptom onset, while also attracting educational use and public discussion. The evidence record is still young, but it already shows a study moving from a high-profile publication into the active research conversation.
